title: Update: My AI-generated arcade shooter (formerly Photon Fighters) is officially released as ZEROVEXIS!
author: ShreddedCheddar32
selftext:
**\*\*Quick note for anyone who saw my earlier post:** This game was previously called *Photon Fighters*. I discovered a naming conflict and rebranded it to **ZEROVEXIS** before the official release. Same project, new name! This is the finished, publicly available version.\*\*



Hey everyone!

I've been experimenting with AI-driven game development, and I just officially released my first commercial game, **ZEROVEXIS**, on itch.io!

It's a twin-stick arcade shooter featuring 10 sectors, 50 encounters, 10 bosses, and a scoring system built around near misses, combos, and enemy vulnerability windows.

Here's the interesting part: **I didn't write the code myself.**

The game was implemented using AI, while I handled the creative direction, gameplay design, testing, balancing, and iteration.

One of the biggest things I've learned is that generating a functional game and making that game genuinely fun are two very different challenges.

A lot of the development process involved playing encounters repeatedly, identifying where combat felt unfair or too easy, adjusting enemy behaviors, and refining how the scoring mechanics interact with combat.

For example, combining near-miss bonuses, combo multipliers, and vulnerability windows created an unexpectedly deep skill ceiling. Skilled players can deliberately take risks, manipulate enemy positioning, and prioritize targets to maximize their scores.

I've attached an uninterrupted 34-second gameplay clip from Sector 7 so you can see the result rather than just screenshots.

**ZEROVEXIS is available for $2.99 on itch.io:**

[https://cheddar32.itch.io/zerovexis](https://cheddar32.itch.io/zerovexis)

I'm especially interested in hearing from other developers experimenting with AI-generated games. How much of your development time ends up going toward iteration and balancing versus the initial code generation?

comments.author: SeasawPhilosopher
comments.body: Looks interesting but the sound is awful, sorry to be blunt but it’s super annoying. There are lots of free sound effects online, like the Sonniss GDC packages. Tell your agent to search for better sound and to pull in some CCO licensed electronic music.

replies.author: ShreddedCheddar32
replies.body:
Thanks for the feedback! No worries about being blunt. That's exactly the kind of thing I want to hear.

I spent a lot of time iterating on the gameplay and balancing, but the audio definitely received less attention. I'll check out the Sonniss libraries you mentioned.

Appreciate you taking a look!

replies.author: SeasawPhilosopher
replies.body: Yeah audio feedback in games makes a huge difference. I was surprised how much just a few hours spent on it improved my game. I downloaded all the Sonniss packages and for my games I just point Claude Code to it and tell it to find sounds for game interactions and make a review page for me to see what I like.

replies.author: ShreddedCheddar32
replies.body:
It's interesting because during all of the hours I spent playing and testing it, the sounds never bothered me, and I'm a musician! In fact, the sounds became an important part of the gameplay, as each one indicates a different event that's happening: a specific enemy attack, a vulnerability window, successful near miss, etc. So, if I decide to change the sound effects, I would definitely still want to keep them in a cohesive style and make sure they still carry uniqueness to each one.

I do think some background music would probably go a long way as well.
